title: Regularities, All the Way Down
author: Becky Allen
summary: Becky Allen (Falsifiable) revisits a 2019 researchED talk in which Kris Boulton argued that 'cognitive science is almost useless for designing effective teaching,' and uses Boulton's career-long struggle to apply Siegfried Engelmann's Direct Instruction theory to secondary mathematics as a case study in the limits of educational theory. She proposes a three-layer hierarchy of 'regularities': the universal layer of general cognitive science (limited working memory, retrieval strengthens memory), the knowledge-type layer where Engelmann operated (classifying content into teachable forms like Basic Concepts, Joinings, Cognitive Routines), and a third, idea-level layer of granular design decisions — which misconception is most likely, which representation should carry the meaning first — that no higher-level theory can resolve. Allen argues it is tempting, for both intellectual and practical reasons, to believe a high-enough theory would make this bottom layer unnecessary, but Boulton's years of work building Unstoppable Learning show that even correctly classifying a topic within Engelmann's system does not tell you how to teach any specific idea. Her conclusion is that teacher development needs to look less like exhortations ('be clear,' 'use retrieval') and more like the slow accumulation of a shared library of idea-specific instructional solutions — work she says AI platforms will only get right if their designers build this idea-level guidance in deliberately rather than assuming it emerges automatically from scale.
points: Allen's central move is to reframe the cognitive-science-vs-instruction debate as a three-layer hierarchy of 'regularities' — universal cognitive science, Engelmann-style knowledge-type classes, and irreducible idea-level design decisions.

Even correctly classifying a topic into one of Engelmann's 'content classes' (per Kris Boulton's application to secondary maths) constrains instruction without ever fully determining it — you still have to decide, e.g., whether to teach 'limit' as a prediction, a tolerance, or a repair.

The temptation to believe a high-enough theory eliminates idea-by-idea design work is both intellectual (pattern-hungry minds want clean rules) and practical (topic-by-topic design is expensive to scale).

Allen argues AI/LLM-based learning platforms will only succeed by explicitly encoding idea-level guidance (misleading intuitions, fragile distinctions, reliable entry routes) rather than assuming scale alone will surface it.

Her practical recommendation for teacher development: build a shared, reusable library of worked solutions to recurring instructional-design problems, rather than relying on high-level exhortations like 'be clear' or 'use retrieval.'
quotes: But underneath the friction, Kris was trying to argue that cognitive scientists give us theories of learning, but not theories of instruction. They tell us how the brain processes information, but they don't tell us what to say to a room of thirty 14-year-olds on a Tuesday morning.

Cognitive science mostly trades in the general laws of the human animal that apply to almost anything worth learning. This is the 'biology' of education. It tells us that working memory is limited and that retrieval strengthens long-term memory.

It is extraordinarily tempting to believe that the higher layers will ultimately make the lower ones unnecessary. There are good reasons for this temptation. One is intellectual: human beings are pattern-hungry.
The difficulty is not that Engelmann's theory is wrong, but rather that 'content classes' constrains instruction, but do not uniquely determine it.

We often hear that education theory has 'failed' because it cannot tell teachers exactly what to do. But the more accurate conclusion is that theory often operates too high up the hierarchy and then over-promises.

Platforms do not succeed through technological development alone; they succeed when they encode the structural features that make particular ideas hard—misleading intuitions, fragile distinctions, and the most reliable entry routes.
